subject: botany_2
question_text: Write short notes on seed dormancy.

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.27, printed question 24. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". BOOK NOTE: the guide names the tomato germination inhibitor "lycopane". The card says "chemical inhibitors present in the seed", which is what NCERT states, and records the guide's word here rather than repeating a name that is not standard.

insider_note: Dormancy and quiescence are a favourite pair. If you have room, add one line saying dormancy is INTERNAL and quiescence is external — it costs nothing and often earns credit.

steps.label: What seed dormancy is
steps.margin_note: Definition, internal cause, and the contrast with quiescence.
lines: Seed dormancy is the inability of a seed to
germinate, or the delay in its germination,
even when conditions are favourable.
It is caused by INTERNAL factors of the seed
itself.
Dormancy differs from QUIESCENCE, where the
seed fails to germinate because the outside
conditions are wrong.
steps.why: The cause being internal is what separates dormancy from quiescence, and that distinction is the whole basis of the answer.
common_mistakes: Saying dormancy is caused by dry or cold weather. That is QUIESCENCE.
Saying a dormant seed is dead. It is alive and will germinate once dormancy is broken.
steps.memory_tip: Dormancy is the seed's own decision; quiescence is the weather's.

steps.label: Causes: the seed coat
steps.margin_note: Name the cause and say what it blocks. Four lines.
lines: 1. HARD SEED COAT:
A tough, impermeable seed coat stops water and
oxygen from entering.
Without water and oxygen the embryo cannot
start growing.
steps.why: Germination begins with the uptake of water, so a coat that keeps water out prevents even the first step.
common_mistakes: Saying the hard coat kills the embryo. It only keeps water and oxygen OUT.
Naming only the coat and stopping. There are other causes to give.
steps.memory_tip: No water in, no germination out.

steps.label: Causes: chemical inhibitors and cold
steps.margin_note: Two more causes with an example each.
lines: 2. CHEMICAL INHIBITORS:
Some seeds, such as tomato, contain chemicals
that stop germination. Abscisic acid is one.
3. NEED FOR CHILLING:
Seeds such as Polygonum will not germinate for
weeks or months until they have been kept cold
and moist.
steps.why: A seed that needs a cold period cannot germinate in autumn, so the chilling requirement is a clock that holds the seedling back until spring.
common_mistakes: Saying the inhibitor is in the soil. It is inside the SEED.
Saying chilling kills dormancy instantly. It takes weeks of cold, moist conditions.
steps.memory_tip: Some seeds carry their own brake; others wait out a winter.

steps.label: Breaking dormancy
steps.margin_note: Both named treatments, matched to their causes, plus the hormone.

lines.text: Scarify the coat, or chill the seed

lines: A hard coat can be broken by SCARIFICATION:
rubbing, chipping or acid treatment.
A chilling requirement is met by
STRATIFICATION, also called prechilling:
layering the seeds in moist sand or peat
through the winter.
Gibberellins also break seed dormancy.
steps.why: Each treatment removes one named cause, so the way dormancy is broken tells you what was causing it.
common_mistakes: Confusing scarification with stratification. Scarification breaks the COAT; stratification supplies the COLD.
Leaving out gibberellins. They are the hormone that breaks dormancy.
steps.memory_tip: Scarify the shell, stratify in the cold.
